evidence_registry.speaker: Charles
evidence_registry.text: You mentioned vetting and qualification. Like what do you look for? Or what do you screen for on that, on the service um provider side?

evidence_registry.speaker: Charles
evidence_registry.text: I've had a virtual assistant. I've had three virtual assistants in the last ten years. And the ones that have worked have worked for exactly the reasons that you've outlined which are that you make sure the client has reasonable expectations and knows how to work with a VA, and you pick high quality people. The challenge I have though is I've never been able to figure how do you use technology to make this better. like I just don't know how these kinds of businesses, even when they're successful, become the kinds of ones where technology gives you a ton of leverage. So this is probably one of the hardest passes I've had to do, cos I like everything about what you said. I like you, your energy. And I think you have the right insights. This is just a business where I struggle to see how technology can give you the kind of leverage I want.

rationales.explanation: Charles asks which vetting and qualification criteria are used on the service-provider side, probing an operational component of the product's success.
Charles explicitly grounds his assessment in having used three virtual assistants over ten years.
He positively identifies reasonable client expectations, client education, and high-quality people as the reasons the service works.
Charles says he likes the founder, her energy, and her insights.
Charles's explicit reason for passing is that he cannot see how technology can provide substantial leverage in this business model.

annotation_summary: Charles's audited Out decision is explicitly driven by his inability to see technology leverage in the virtual-assistant business, despite positive assessments of the founder and the service's operating principles.
